Tier 2Standing interpretationhuman analysis that cannot be computed, so each item is dated and carries a review-by. Figures marked ⟳ are still recomputed every build; the judgement around them is not.
The account has ACOS headroom; specific SKUs do not.

Break-even ACOS is 39.2% TCN / 28.5% WWB pre-labor, 29.9% / 25.8% with labor loaded. The account runs 24.3%, so there is headroom in aggregate — but the aggregate is not where the money leaks. 86010L is spending at 60.0% ACOS ($1,476 in the window) against a ~10% margin, well past break-even on either basis. The single worst offender today is 45001-L at 92.6%.

Basis: Break-even ACOS comes from CostSmith's margin work and is NOT computed in this database — treat it as an input, not a measurement. Account and per-SKU ACOS are recomputed here every build. 86010L is PINNED, because the ~10% margin claim was measured against that SKU and must not silently follow whichever SKU is worst on a given night.

WWB chicory returns far above the account and is barely spending.

WWB_French Chicory_Chicory_CAT_[Chicory - Broad]_SP (Sponsored Products) returned $21.53 per ad dollar on only $284 of trailing-30d spend — 9% of the $3,000 its $100/day cap allows. Compare the whole account at 24.3% ACOS. Because it is nowhere near its cap, the binding constraint is bids and targeting, not budget: raising the daily budget alone would change nothing. Still the clearest reallocation candidate in the account.

Basis: Campaign-grain trailing-30d spend and 14-day attributed sales from raw_amazon_ads_campaigns; budget is the campaign's DAILY cap x 30. Restated 2026-08-05 against the data: the original note called this a Sponsored BRANDS campaign returning ~$3.79/dollar on a 'starved $630/mo budget'. It is Sponsored PRODUCTS, the return is far higher, $630 was a trailing-30d SPEND figure on a different WWB chicory campaign rather than a budget, and the cap is not binding at all — so the recommended action changes from 'raise the budget' to 'raise bids / widen targeting'.

Pickers are clamped to the window Amazon actually has data for: 2026-04-30 → 2026-08-22 (115 days). The Advertising API retains reports only ~60–95 days, so 2026-04-30 is a permanent floor — the window can only grow forward, never backward. Before that date there is no data, which is not the same as $0 spend: impressions, clicks and spend all began being captured on 2026-04-30 and the earlier history is unrecoverable at any price. Everything on this page — tiles, charts, the monthly, ad-product, per-SKU and campaign tables — recomputes on the selected range.

Spend & attributed ad sales
Ad spend
Attributed ad sales

Shown as small multiples rather than one plot: ad sales run ~7× spend, so a shared axis flattened the spend line into noise. Each panel keeps its own scale and the same x range — and no information is lost, because the spend-to-sales ratio is exactly what the ACOS chart below plots. Ad sales are Amazon’s attributed sales for clicks on these ads, not total Amazon revenue.

Efficiency — ACOS vs TACOS
ACOS TACOS

Both are percentages, so they share one axis. ACOS = spend ÷ ad-attributed sales (how the ads themselves perform). TACOS = spend ÷ total Amazon sales (how much of the whole channel ad spend consumes) — the cross-table metric Amazon’s own console can’t show, since total sales come from SP-API. ROAS is deliberately not plotted: it is the exact reciprocal of ACOS.

Per-SKU ad performance ()
click a column to sort
Product Ad spend Ad sales ACOS Units Clicks Same-SKU

Product names come from raw_amazon_inventory.product_name, joined on the advertised ASIN. Amazon titles are 65–232-character SEO strings, so each row shows a derived short label with the SKU and ASIN beneath it and the full untruncated title on hover. A SKU with no title renders as the bare SKU with an italic “name not in inventory feed” — never blanked, never dropped.

Name coverage in this table is 201 of 201 SKUs (100%). A coverage check across advertised ASINs reads lower (190 of 229) because 39 of those 229 are not Amazon ASINs at all — see the retailer note at the foot of this page. Every row that can appear here is SKU-keyed and Amazon, so the italic fallback above is defensive (for a SKU advertised before the next inventory snapshot lands) rather than something you should expect to see today.

From the spAdvertisedProduct report level — ad cost attributed to the specific SKU/ASIN advertised. Same-SKU is the share of that SKU’s ad sales which were actually the advertised product; the remainder is halo (the click sold something else), which is why per-SKU ACOS alone overstates how well a SKU converts itself. SKU identity here is Amazon’s seller SKU — join to CatalogSmith’s product master for margin, rather than matching on these strings directly (pack/channel suffixes such as L mean a naive join double-counts).

CVR = ad orders ÷ clicks. Campaign totals honour the date range above — they are rolled up in the browser from per-day campaign rows, so this table can never disagree with the tiles and charts. Budget/day and Status are current campaign settings, not window aggregates. A campaign with no spend inside the selected range drops out of the table.

Retailer note. Amazon Advertising also serves Sponsored Products on non-Amazon retailers, and those rows arrive in the same report. Teeccino runs 15 iherb.com campaigns alongside 114 Amazon ones (no campaign belongs to both). They are 0.98% of ad spend ($1,884 of $192,802) and are included in the totals, charts and campaign table above, tagged iherb.com. They carry an iHerb product id in place of an ASIN and no Amazon seller SKU, so they never reach the per-SKU table — that is the entire reason an ASIN-level name-coverage check reads 190 of 229 while this page’s SKU-level coverage is 201 of 201.

Source: raw_amazon_ads_campaigns + calc_daily_amazon_ads (Amazon Advertising API, Reporting v3, profile 35319265126281 / US). TACOS joins ad spend to SP-API total Amazon sales in calc_daily_amazon_net. Owned by DataOps; paid-ad strategy is AdSmith’s lane.

Monthly revenue & ad spend
Revenue Ad spend

Both series are dollars, so one axis is honest here. Revenue is Amazon gross principal for this SKU; ad spend is what was spent advertising it. The final month is month-to-date, so its dip is incomplete data, not a decline.

Monthly ACOS & TACOS
ACOS TACOS

ACOS = ad spend ÷ ad-attributed sales. TACOS = ad spend ÷ this SKU’s total Amazon revenue — so it shows how much of the product’s whole business the ads consume, including sales the ads never touched. The final month is month-to-date. Ad spend only exists from 2026-04 onward (Amazon’s report retention), so earlier months show revenue with no ACOS.
